Photograph: Joel Lindhe/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Johan Forssell, the migration minister, said the European Commission was onboard with Sweden’s approach. Photograph: Joel Lindhe/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Sweden Swedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of Britons Minister says Sweden has ‘fulfilled its commitments’ amid criticism of ‘unjust’ decisions such as case of Joyce Thomas Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Wed 2 Sep 2026 08.59 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 09.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Swedish government has doubled down on its position on removing and deporting British citizens on the grounds they were late to apply for permission to stay after Brexit . The migration minister, Johan Forssell, issued a robust defence of the Swedish migration agency’s implementation of the Brexit withdrawal agreement on Wednesday in response to a question from an MP about the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has been ordered to leave the country after 21 years . Forssell said the European Commission , which is legally mandated to ensure EU member states implement the withdrawal agreement correctly, was onboard with Sweden’s approach. “The migration board has followed up on the application of the withdrawal agreement and the assessment is that Sweden has fulfilled its commitments. This assessment is shared by the commission,” he said. There has been growing controversy over removal orders issued to British citizens who did not know that Sweden was one of 13 countries in the EU that required formal applications to stay in the country post-Brexit. British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhood Read more In another case, a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, has been deported despite having lived in Sweden since he was 10 . Thomas’s local MP, Häkan Svenneling, of the Left party, told the Guardian: “It seems to me that the Swedish government thinks everything is fine even though British citizens are being deported from Sweden right now. Not acting is also an action in this situation. What Sweden needs is a new government and a new migration minister who stops deporting people with strong connections to Sweden.” In his written answer to Svenneling, Forssell offered British citizens facing deportation a sliver of hope. He said: “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future.” View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, has been ordered to leave Sweden after living there for 21 years. Photograph: Felix Andler Thomas has been told she must remove herself from Sweden by Tuesday 8 September or face deportation and a potential ban from the Schengen area. She is one of several British citizens who have been faced with removal orders after the migration agency rejected their late applications to stay. The UK Foreign Office has raised Sweden’s approach to late applications for post-Brexit residency a number of times in the specialised committee on citizens’ rights, a structure set up to ensure the withdrawal agreement is implemented properly. David Milstead, who runs the grassroots organisation Brits in Sweden, said the Swedish response was not a surprise. “The government was hardly going to disown the decisions of [the migration agency] or the Swedish courts. The real question is whether Sweden’s approach is consistent with EU law and the [withdrawal agreement],” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion He pointed out that under the agreement, the UK was obliged to set up a statutory body, the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), to independently ensure the Home Office implemented the Brexit deal correctly, while the European Commission performed the correspondent role for EU member states. “The IMA has taken a much more robust approach. It is hard to imagine it not challenging the UK had it operated a policy like Sweden’s, which would have put the rights of around a quarter of a million successful late applicants [in the UK] at risk,” Milstead said. “Sweden’s approach now needs either to be tested before the European court of justice or addressed through measures that remedy the problem. The government’s response leaves open the possibility of change, and that must include fixing unjust deportation decisions.” The European Commission has been approached for comment. According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025 a total of 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. Analysis by the Foreign Office found this was 32.9% of the 7,565 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU member states over this period. Although it is not possible to determine exactly how many were in Sweden prior to the end of the UK-EU transition period, it is likely that the majority will have been. Thomas has been in Sweden for 21 years and says her late husband inquired about the impact of Brexit and was told by the authorities there was nothing they needed to do to remain in the country legally. The couple moved to the country to be close to their son and grandchildren, and Thomas said she had been left feeling sick with worry after receiving the removal order. https://www.politico.eu/article/sweden-e.text: STOCKHOLM — Former center-left Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson is on course to retake power in Sweden as exit polling suggests a right-wing alliance that includes the far right is falling short. Andersson, the leader of the Social Democrats, spent much of the election campaign warning voters against handing ministerial posts to what she called an “extremist” party with “neo-Nazi” roots — the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. If the surveys prove accurate, it would mean rejection for incumbent PM Ulf Kristersson. The conservative Moderate party leader had decided to work closely with the Sweden Democrats and promised to give them seats in cabinet for the first time if he won. Advertisement Advertisement Two separate exit polls for Sweden’s SVT public broadcaster and TV4 showed Andersson’s left bloc on track to take 51% of the vote. (Sweden’s electoral system is based on proportional representation.) Kristersson’s alliance on the right was projected to win 47%. Exit polls have not always been accurate in the past, but the picture should become clearer later on Sunday night when broadcasters are expected to announce updated forecasts after a critical mass of districts declare results. Whoever ends up winning, party leaders will take weeks to finalize a new coalition agreement. “Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her dark red campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.” With the prospect of the far right entering government for the first time, the vote marks a watershed moment for Sweden that will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other populist nationalist parties are gaining ground. Even Andersson accepts that a victory for her left bloc would not consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final result is a narrow one. “The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said. Advertisement Advertisement But victory would be a major relief for the Social Democrat leader and her political allies in other parties on the left of Swedish politics. Andersson was thrown out of office in an election four years ago, and spent the intervening period leading the opposition. For months, her bloc — which includes the Left Party, with its communist roots, as well as the Greens — had enjoyed a comfortable advantage in the polls. But that lead narrowed dramatically in the last two weeks of the campaign, with one poll on the eve of the vote putting the two rival blocs in a dead heat. Kristersson’s allies on the right may be left wondering whether he made a mistake in seeking to collaborate so closely with such controversial partners in the far-right Sweden Democrats and their leader Jimmie Åkesson. The PM told POLITICO he trusted Åkesson because the two had worked well together for four years, with the Sweden Democrats supporting the government in parliament without having ministers formally in the cabinet. Kristersson and Åkesson tried to persuade voters they deserved another term to finish the work they started — especially bringing down violent crime and reducing immigration. But Andersson argued that many voters had balked at moves by the Kristersson government to expel young people from the country who had attended Swedish schools, spoke the language fluently and made their lives in Sweden. “People think that’s stupid and inhumane,” she told POLITICO on Sunday. It didn’t help Kristersson’s cause that his side was forced to fight claims of Russian infiltration in the final days of the campaign. In an earlier interview with POLITICO , Andersson demanded that Kristersson come clean about allegations that the partner of a senior Sweden Democrats official had promoted pro-Russian narratives and linked up with a Russian state group. Advertisement Advertisement Speaking to POLITICO on Friday, Kristersson argued that the real security risk lay with Andersson’s allies — given that two of the parties she may end up governing with had opposed Sweden’s NATO membership before the country joined the alliance. Jan Teorell, a professor of political science at Stockholm University, said the center left had tried hard to make the election a referendum on allowing the far right to share power. “This is definitely part of what the Social Democrats in particular want the election to be about,” he said. The gap between the leftwing camp and Kristersson’s bloc, including the Sweden Democrats, opened up after the latter two agreed to work together in 2022, according to Teorell. That “could be interpreted as dissatisfaction among some center-right voters with either SD, the agreement as such, or both, making them switch to the other side.” However, it won’t be clear why Sweden turned away from the far right until detailed voter behavior studies are published after the election, he said. WARSAW, Ind. -- The MedTech Expo is taking place in Warsaw. Seen as the orthopedic capital; many around the world gathered in Indiana to display or present different medical technology. Plug and Play helps life science and medical device companies, offering them opportunity to present their product and put them through their accelerator program. Different medical technologies were pitched in front of 200 people seeing hands-on technology demonstrations. Through all this, Plug and Play looks for the best technology startups to connect with large corporations around the world. Some of the companies' pitches focused on infection technology and AI enabled surgical tools. "Yeah. So, we have startups in in medical device or medical technologies coming across a lot of different areas. It could be sensor technologies, implants, wearables. And what they did is they were from around the world. They came in today to pitch and present at the culmination of our accelerator program, which is a 3-to-4-month accelerator program that we run here in Warsaw, Indiana on behalf of our global accelerator program of Plug and Play." says Plug and Play Director Brandon Noll. A NSW parliamentary inquiry into Redeemer Baptist school has found the western Sydney school breached basic child safeguarding standards. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen NSW Greens MP and committee chair Abigail Boyd speaks to media in Sydney on Tuesday. A NSW parliamentary inquiry into Redeemer Baptist school has found the western Sydney school breached basic child safeguarding standards. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Sydney Sydney private school accused of mishandling sexual abuse allegations should be banned from enrolling new students, inquiry says Inquiry recommends police investigate allegations of sexual assault and other abuse at Redeemer Baptist school Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Mon 9 Nov 2026 23.51 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 02.13 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An investigation into a private religious school accused of mishandling allegations of sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse has recommended it be barred from enrolling new students. Former students and teachers of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist school told a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry about a string of disturbing allegations. They included students being made to share beds with teachers and its principal once wandering naked through a common area. In a report tabled in state parliament on Tuesday, a committee found the school – run by the Redeemer Baptist Church – breached basic child safeguarding standards. Sexual assault allegations were not handled appropriately and the school put children at significant risk of harm, the committee found. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email It also found staff at the school lacked essential workplace rights and failed to satisfy basic standards of good governance. The committee recommended the school be prevented from enrolling new students while it was under investigation by the NSW Education Standards Authority. It also recommended the allegations raised in the inquiry be investigated by NSW police and the office of the children’s guardian. The committee chair and Greens MP, Abigail Boyd, noted the school was subjected to parliamentary scrutiny in 2006, but no procedures had been put in place to monitor what was clearly a “high-risk situation”. View image in fullscreen Redeemer Baptist school in Parramatta. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP She said it was thanks to the bravery of those who had spoken out that the committee had enough evidence to make its strong findings and recommendations. The school received about $6m a year in government funding, Boyd said, and had enough cash to launch legal challenges against those who raised their voices against the religious group. “They also have deep political ties with both state and federal politicians,” she told parliament. People who had escaped the school appeared to be absolutely terrified of its leaders, Boyd said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “When you know that leaving means leaving with no financial assets, and when you have finally managed to escape, it’s no wonder that you would be terrified of your abuser,” she said in parliament. The committee lashed a lack of regulatory oversight, including from the education authority, suggesting a number of alarming matters needed proper investigation. They included allegations of persistent Centrelink fraud and dodgy tax practices. “It is, at the very least, troubling that an asset-rich, seemingly prosperous school operates by withholding wages from its workforce, who claim benefits, while the school receives millions of dollars in public funding,” the report said. A Redeemer Baptist school spokesperson previously said the school had fully cooperated with the relevant regulators. “Redeemer Baptist School takes its child safety obligations extremely seriously and has an unblemished record of compliance with state and federal regulators for 45 years,” they said. The school did not immediately respond to a request for comment following the report’s release.
